extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theory and public opinion
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and analysis of how public opinion and a 'common will' are formed, including the roles of economic position, instincts, symbols, rhetoric, and mass communication. Useful for political theorists, historians, and communicators studying persuasion and mass politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of economic/materialistic determinism
rubrics_metrics.description: The materialistic conception of politics cannot predict which of a man's many social relations is effecting a particular opinion; without special inquiry you cannot tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that individuals occupy multiple economic relations (landlord/tenant, employer/employee, creditor/debtor, owner of shares, etc.) and that economic position alone does not determine a fixed set of opinions. Includes examples (owners resisting dispossession but unforeseeable stances on long vs. short views), and historical counterexamples (Marx and Lenin's mistaken predictions about where socialism would arise). Emphasizes need for empirical inquiry rather than assuming determinism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class interests are variable and not unitary
rubrics_metrics.description: A class interest can be conceived largely or narrowly, selfishly or unselfishly, in light of no facts, some facts, many facts, truth and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that because members of a class conceive their interest in diverse ways, the Marxian assumption of a coherent class interest that will produce uniform action is false. Even communal ownership would not eliminate conflicts if people interpret shared conditions differently. Uses this to criticize simplistic remedies for class conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior is not fatally determined by instinct; instincts are shaped by experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Innate dispositions are immersed in experience from infancy and are initiated by perceptions and ideas as well as direct stimuli; repeated acts cease to be 'blind' instincts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draws on James and McDougall: instincts retain a central specific character but cognitive and affective aspects complicate responses. Example: man has instinct of fear but what he fears and how he escapes is determined by experience. Concludes social actions are learned and malleable across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditioned emotional transferability enables symbolic coalitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions attached to one idea can be aroused by substitute stimuli and can be satisfied by substitute responses; a single symbol can unite disparate emotions and motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how a symbol (e.g., 'Americanism') can be read differently by different people yet arouse the same underlying emotion, thereby amalgamating conflicting factions. Examples include Lincoln, Roosevelt, Progressivism, Law and Order. Symbols function as junctions where many roads converge; capturing a symbol allows control of public feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vague, ambiguous language in public appeals to unify heterogeneous audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers deliberately employ language that 'means all things to all men' to avoid explosive points and to bind diverse supporters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Mr. Hughes' 1916 speech: use of 'correct principles', stretching of 'intervention' and 'American rights' to cover divergent meanings for different factions, and treating contentious items as if they did not exist (obliteration) when compromise is impossible. Vagueness is presented as a common technical method for creating a vote out of conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution and shorthand in political thought; danger of verbalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Because people simplify complex situations by substituting names, signs, and samples, they risk forgetting the substitution and lapse into talking about names regardless of objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that shorthand is necessary for practical thought but if one forgets that names are substitutes for complex realities, misalliances occur and reasoning becomes divorced from actual objects. This is a cognitive hazard in politics where complex realities are constantly simplified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion is first-hand while cognition and conation are often indirect
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals experience the emotion directly, but the stimulus (facts) and the response (effects) are often mediated and remote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the starving child example: the spectator's desire to help is real though the perception of the child and the effectiveness of his action (giving money to an organization) are indirect. Emphasizes that the emotional experience, not accurate cognition or direct action, often drives political behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern mass communication enables coordinated formation of a 'common consciousness'
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies like cable, radio, telegraph, and daily press make simultaneous exposure possible and allow leaders to attempt to knit together ideas across populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: President Wilson's Fourteen Points were an attempt to exploit modern communications to start a return to a 'common consciousness' across nations during WWI. The argument stresses the historical novelty and power of modern media to shape collective understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion often crystallizes as the least common denominator after contradictory motives cancel
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate political decisions (e.g., election outcomes) can reflect a simple minimal agreement (e.g., 'change parties') even though individual motives were varied and conflicting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown by the 1920 U.S. election: diverse reasons among Republicans/Democrats cancelled into a simple desire to replace one party with another; elected officials then face public opinions that are not identical to the motives that produced them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political leaders secure alliances by capturing and deploying current symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: A leader or interest that captures the symbols by which public feeling is contained controls the approaches of public policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses struggle to possess symbols (Lincoln, Roosevelt) and the tactical advantages of doing so. Also notes limits: extreme abuse of what the symbol represents can 'burst' it and destroy its unifying power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols have limits — abuse or resistance can break their unifying power
rubrics_metrics.description: Too violent abuse of what a symbol is thought to represent, or excessive resistance under the name of that symbol to new purposes, will 'burst' the symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives historical example: the symbol of Holy Russia and the Little Father burst under suffering and defeat in 1917. Serves as caution that reliance on symbols is contingent and fragile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political technique: select non-explosive initial themes to build coalition
rubrics_metrics.description: To unite factions divided on explosive matters, a speaker should pick opening subjects that are non-explosive and serve as binders, then slide toward broader coalition-building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Mr. Hughes selecting the spoils system in diplomatic appointments as an opening theme that avoided the explosive conflicts of 1912 and 1916, using stereotypes and 'binders' (e.g., invoking Lincoln) to heal schisms and amalgamate varied factions.
